# Introduction to Ezekiel

## Part 1: General Introduction

### Outline of Ezekiel

1. Yahweh calls Ezekiel to speak his words (1:1–3:27)
2. Yahweh judges Judah and Jerusalem (4:1–24:27)
3. Ezekiel prophesies against nearby nations (25:1–32:32)
4. Yahweh explains the fall of Jerusalem (33:1–33)
5. Ezekiel brings messages of hope (34:1–48:35)
  A. A new shepherd (34:1–31)
  B. Edom destroyed (35:1–15)
  C. Israel restored (36:1–37:28)
  D. Gog and Magog (38:1–39:29)
  E. Jerusalem and the temple restored (40:1–48:35)

### What is Ezekiel about?

The book of Ezekiel contains messages that Ezekiel prophesied between 593 B.C. and 571 B.C. The Jewish people, including Ezekiel, were exiled in Babylonia. Ezekiel told them that God was punishing them because they had sinned against him. He also said that God was going to further punish them by destroying Jerusalem and his temple. This happened in 586 B.C. After that, God gave Ezekiel messages that assured the people that God would restore them to their land. He said that God was using Babylon to punish them, but that eventually another nation would defeat the Babylonians. Ezekiel also prophesied about how God would restore Jerusalem and the temple so that the people could worship and sacrifice to him again. Ezekiel then described how the land would be divided again among the tribes of Israel.

### How should the title of this book be translated?

“Ezekiel” or “The Book of Ezekiel” is the traditional name for this book. Translators may also call it “The Messages from God Brought by Ezekiel.”

### Who wrote the book of Ezekiel?

Ezekiel wrote the prophecies in the book of Ezekiel. He was a prophet and priest who lived near Babylon in the time of the exile.

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

### What was Ezekiel’s temple?

Several chapters of the book of Ezekiel give a detailed description of a new temple that Ezekiel sees in a vision. However, the temple that the people built after going back to Jerusalem was much smaller. Because Ezekiel’s temple has never been built, some scholars think that this temple is to be built in the future. Others think that it is a description of the heavenly, ideal temple. Other scholars think that Ezekiel’s temple is symbolic of the Church.

### Do the sacrifices in Ezekiel follow the law of Moses?

The sacrifices in Ezekiel 46 are somewhat different than the required sacrifices in Numbers 28. This may be because Ezekiel prophesied about a new temple with new sacrifices.

## Part 3: Important Translation Issues

### How should one represent Ezekiel’s visions in translation?

The book of Ezekiel has many complicated visions. These were things that God showed to Ezekiel, and many of them were visions of supernatural beings that are beyond human experience. Translators should avoid trying to explain these visions in their translations. Instead, they should present the visions just as they are in the source text. In some of the visions, God transported Ezekiel to other places. It seems clear that God allowed Ezekiel to see these places without physically going there.

### What does “know that I am Yahweh” mean?

This is a common phrase in the book of Ezekiel. Yahweh makes this statement after announcing either a severe punishment for people’s sin or a miraculous event in which he saves and restores his people. The phrase means that, after experiencing one of these things, the people will know who Yahweh is in the sense that he has all power and is in complete control of history. Since Yahweh announces the disaster or rescue ahead of when it happens, this also means that the people will know that Yahweh always does what he promises to do. Translate this phrase consistently throughout the book.

### “son of man”

The phrase “son of man” translates simply to “mortal man” or “human being,” reminding Ezekiel that despite receiving extraordinary divine visions, he remains a creature dependent on God. By repeatedly calling Ezekiel this throughout this book, Yahweh establishes a clear boundary between his infinite glory and the messenger’s earthly limitations.

### “spirit,” “breath,” or “wind”

The same Hebrew word can mean either “spirit,” “breath,” or “wind.” In biblical times, the concept of a person’s spirit was closely related to the concept of a person’s breath. The term can also refer to wind, that is, the movement of air in the natural world. Often there will be a note recommending how to translate this in specific contexts and the translation team will need to decide how to translate it in each case.

# Ezekiel 1 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

1. Ezekiel sees Yahweh’s glorious appearance (1–14)
2. Ezekiel sees the living creatures and heavenly wheels (15–21)
3. Ezekiel sees the glory of Yahweh above the throne (22–28)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The exile

Ezekiel prophesied in Babylonia. When he mentions living “among the exiles,” he means he was one of the Israelite people whom the Babylonians had forcibly removed from the land of Judah. He begins the book describing visions he saw five years after the exile of King Jehoiachin.
2:
# Ezekiel 2 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

1. Yahweh calls Ezekiel to speak to rebellious Israel (1–5)
2. Yahweh strengthens Ezekiel against their opposition (6–8)
3. Yahweh gives Ezekiel his words to proclaim (9–10)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### A house of rebellion

Yahweh repeatedly calls Israel “a house of rebellion,” picturing the people as a household marked by refusal to obey him.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### The unnamed speaker

The speaker is never named although it is referring to the previous chapter to the one seated on the throne which is assumed to be Yahweh.

# Ezekiel 3 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter completes the commissioning of Ezekiel that began in chapter 2, and it ends with the prophet confined to his house and unable to speak unless Yahweh gives him a message.

1. Yahweh commissions Ezekiel as a watchman (1–11)
2. Yahweh’s Spirit strengthens and guides Ezekiel (12–15)
3. Yahweh holds Ezekiel responsible for warning the wicked (16–21)
4. Yahweh reveals his glory and commands Ezekiel to speak (22–27)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Eating the scroll

Yahweh commands Ezekiel to eat a scroll, and it tastes as sweet as honey. This symbolic act represents the prophet taking Yahweh’s message into himself, so that the words he speaks are Yahweh’s words and not his own.

### The prophet as a watchman

A watchman guarded an ancient city by looking out for danger and warning the people. In the same way, Ezekiel must warn the people of Yahweh’s judgment, and Yahweh holds him accountable for the death of anyone whom he fails to warn.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### The unnamed speaker

Yahweh is identified only as “he” for most of the chapter, since his speech continues from the vision of chapters 1–2. If it would be helpful in your language, you could name the speaker at the start of each section.

# Ezekiel 4 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh commands Ezekiel to perform a series of symbolic actions that portray the coming siege of Jerusalem and the famine that will accompany it.

1. Yahweh commands Ezekiel to portray Jerusalem’s siege (1–3)
2. Ezekiel bears Israel’s guilt and judgment (4–8)
3. Ezekiel portrays the famine and suffering of Jerusalem (9–17)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Symbolic actions

Ezekiel does not merely announce the siege of Jerusalem; he acts it out with a brick, an iron griddle, and his own body. Such enacted signs were a recognized form of prophecy and were understood to portray what Yahweh was about to do.

### Bearing iniquity

When Ezekiel “carries the iniquity” of Israel and of Judah, he is not being punished for his own sin. He is publicly representing the guilt of the people and the punishment that it deserves.

### Unclean food

The law of Moses forbade certain foods and required that food be prepared in ways that kept a person ritually pure. Baking bread over human excrement would defile both the food and the prophet, which is why Ezekiel protests in 4:14.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Instructions to Ezekiel

Yahweh gives most of his instructions in this chapter with a Hebrew verb form that the ULT renders as “you shall.” These are instructions rather than predictions. Translate this form with the most natural way in your language for giving instructions.

### Weights and measures

The chapter states Ezekiel’s daily ration in shekels and in a fraction of a hin. You could keep these ancient units and explain them in a note, or you could give modern equivalents, as the UST does.

# Ezekiel 5 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter completes the series of symbolic actions that began in chapter 4 and then interprets them.

1. Yahweh judges Jerusalem for its rebellion (1–4)
2. Yahweh declares judgment because of Jerusalem’s abominations (5–10)
3. Yahweh brings famine, death, and scattering upon Jerusalem (11–17)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Symbolic actions

Ezekiel acts out the coming judgment rather than only announcing it. Shaving the head and beard was in itself a sign of mourning and humiliation, and each portion of the hair stands for a group of the people, as Yahweh explains in 5:12.

### Defiling the sanctuary

Yahweh gives as a reason for this judgment that the people have brought detestable things into his temple. To make the sanctuary unclean was to treat as common the one place that Yahweh had set apart for himself.

### The curses of the covenant

Famine, the sword, plague, wild animals, and parents eating their own children are the very punishments that Yahweh had warned of in the law of Moses if his people broke the covenant. The first hearers would have recognized these disasters as covenant curses rather than as random calamities.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Shifting addressees

Yahweh addresses Ezekiel in verses 1–4 with a singular “you.” From verse 7 on, he addresses the city of Jerusalem and its people, and the “you” is sometimes singular and sometimes plural, occasionally within a single verse. You may need to make the addressee explicit, as the UST does.

### Quotations within quotations

The whole chapter is speech that Yahweh makes to Ezekiel, and within it he repeatedly introduces further quoted speech with “Thus says the Lord Yahweh.” If these nested quotations would be confusing, you could translate the inner quotations as indirect speech.

### Expressions for anger

The ULT preserves the Hebrew words for anger literally, speaking of Yahweh’s “nose” and his “heat” in 5:13 and 5:15. Many languages will need ordinary words for anger and wrath here, as the UST has.

# Ezekiel 6 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter Yahweh tells Ezekiel to prophesy against the mountains of Israel, where the people worshiped idols.

1. Judgment on the places of idol worship (1–7)
    1. Yahweh commands Ezekiel to speak to the mountains of Israel (1–3)
    2. Yahweh will destroy the altars and leave the dead lying in front of the idols (4–7)
2. Some people will survive and remember Yahweh in exile (8–10)
3. Ezekiel is to lament over Israel’s coming destruction (11–14)
    1. The people will die by sword, famine, and plague (11–12)
    2. The dead will lie among the idols, and the land will become desolate (13–14)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### High places

The high places were hilltop sites where the Israelites built altars and set up idols to worship. Yahweh addresses the mountains, hills, stream beds, and valleys because that is where this idol worship took place, and he will defile those sites with the bodies of the people who worshiped there.

### Idolatry as prostitution

In 6:9 Yahweh speaks of the people’s idol worship as if it were prostitution, that is, sexual unfaithfulness to him. This comparison appears often in Ezekiel.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Yahweh speaks to Ezekiel, telling him to speak to the mountains, and in that speech Ezekiel quotes Yahweh, who again tells Ezekiel what to say, so the chapter has up to four levels of quotation. See [Quotes within Quotes](ta:figs-quotesinquotes) for ways to make this clear.

### The identity of “you”

In verses 2 and 3, Yahweh tells Ezekiel to address his prophecy to the mountains of Israel. In verse 3, he begins speaking to the mountains using a plural “you” and “your.” The real audience for the prophecy is, of course, the people of Israel, and by verse 8 “you” has to refer to the people, so the two “audiences” have become blended. To make this clearer, you may wish to have “you” refer to the people throughout the chapter, as in the UST.

### “You will know that I am Yahweh”

This statement recurs throughout the chapter and the book. It means that when Yahweh carries out his judgment, the people will recognize that he is the true God who has all power and who does what he says. Translate it the same way each time it occurs.

# Ezekiel 7 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a prophecy in poetic language announcing that the end has come for the land of Israel.

1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to announce the end of the land of Israel (1–4)
2. The day of judgment is coming (5–13)
    1. The end has come because of the people’s ways (5–9)
    2. The day has arrived, and buying and selling will no longer matter (10–13)
3. The people will be helpless and will mourn (14–18)
4. Their wealth will not save them, and foreigners will defile Yahweh’s temple (19–22)
5. Yahweh will bring the nations, and no leader will be able to help (23–27)

Some translations set lines of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 7:2–27.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The day of Yahweh

Throughout this chapter, “the end,” “the time,” and “the day” refer to the time when Yahweh will punish the people of Israel for their sins.

### Mourning practices

In this culture, people expressed grief by wearing sackcloth and shaving their heads (v. 18). Ezekiel uses these practices to show how the people will mourn when Yahweh judges them.

### Ritual uncleanness

In verses 19–20, Yahweh compares the people’s silver and gold to the impurity of menstruation. Under the law of Moses, menstruation made a person ritually unclean as well as physically unclean, so the comparison shows that the people will regard their wealth as something that kept them from God and therefore as something detestable to be thrown away.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Repeated refrain

Verses 3–4 and 8–9 are nearly identical, and several sections end with “Then you will know that I am Yahweh.” Translators may want to translate these repeated statements in the same way each time.

### Changes in who is addressed

The word “you” sometimes refers to the land of Israel (feminine singular), sometimes to its inhabitants addressed as one person (masculine singular), and sometimes to the people as a group (plural). Many languages will express all of these as references to the people of Israel.

# Ezekiel 8 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a vision that continues through chapter 11. Yahweh takes Ezekiel to the temple in Jerusalem and shows him a series of increasingly serious abominations that the people are committing there.

1. Ezekiel is carried in a vision from his house to Jerusalem (1–4)
2. Yahweh shows Ezekiel abominations in the temple (5–16)
    1. The image of jealousy north of the altar gate (5–6)
    2. Seventy elders burning incense to carved images (7–13)
    3. Women weeping for Tammuz (14–15)
    4. Twenty-five men worshiping the sun (16)
3. Yahweh says that he will punish them without pity (17–18)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Ezekiel’s vision of Jerusalem

Ezekiel was living among the exiles in Babylonia. He did not travel to Jerusalem physically; he saw the temple and what was happening there in a vision from God (v. 3).

### Idolatry in the temple

The temple was the place where the people were to worship only Yahweh, but the people of Judah were worshiping images of false gods there. For example, the “image of jealousy” was an idol that provoked Yahweh to be jealous (v. 3). Tammuz was a god of the Babylonians and other peoples, for whom women performed ritual weeping (v. 14). The men in verse 16 turned their backs on the temple to bow down to the sun.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Increasingly serious abominations

Each time Yahweh shows Ezekiel an abomination, he says that Ezekiel will see even greater ones (vv. 6, 13, 15). Translators will want to translate this repeated statement the same way each time so that readers can see that each scene is worse than the one before.

# Ezekiel 9 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the vision that began in [Ezekiel 8](ta:08). Yahweh responds to the abominations that he showed Ezekiel in the temple by sending agents to punish Jerusalem.

1. Yahweh summons six executioners and a man clothed in linen (1–2)
2. Yahweh commands the man to mark the faithful and the others to kill everyone else (3–7)
3. Ezekiel pleads for the remnant, and Yahweh answers that he will not spare them (8–10)
4. The man clothed in linen reports that he has done what Yahweh commanded (11)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The glory of God leaving the cherub

In 9:3, the glory of God moves from above the cherubs to the threshold of the temple. These cherubs would be the ones on the top of the ark of the covenant in the innermost sanctuary (Holy of Holies) in the temple. This is the first stage of a movement that continues in chapters 10 and 11, where God’s glory leaves the temple and then the city.

### The mark on the foreheads

The man clothed in linen puts a mark on the people who grieve over the abomination in the city, and the executioners must not harm anyone who has this mark. The mark identifies these people so that they will be protected, because they are true worshipers of Yahweh. The text does not say what the mark looked like, so a general word for “mark” is best.

### Judgment beginning at the sanctuary

Yahweh tells the executioners to begin at his sanctuary and to fill its courts with dead bodies. Dead bodies made a place ritually unclean, so this command shows that, because of the people’s sin, Yahweh was no longer treating the temple as holy.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Ezekiel’s report of a vision

Everything in this chapter is part of the vision that Ezekiel describes. God is showing these things to Ezekiel in Jerusalem without Ezekiel physically being in Jerusalem. The pronoun “he” in [9:1](ta:09) refers to Yahweh, who has been speaking to Ezekiel since chapter 8, so make sure this is clear in your translation.
10:
# Ezekiel 10 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the vision that began in [Ezekiel 8](ta:08). The man clothed in linen carries out Yahweh’s command to scatter burning coals over Jerusalem, and the glory of Yahweh moves farther away from the temple.

1. Yahweh commands the man clothed in linen to take burning coals from among the cherubs (1–8)
    1. Yahweh gives the command (1–2)
    2. The cloud and the glory of Yahweh fill the temple and its courtyard (3–5)
    3. A cherub gives fire to the man (6–8)
2. Ezekiel describes the cherubs and their wheels (9–17)
3. The glory of Yahweh leaves the threshold and stops at the east gate (18–19)
4. Ezekiel recognizes these cherubs as the beings that he saw by the river of Kebar (20–22)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The glory of Yahweh leaving the temple

The glory of Yahweh moved to the threshold of the temple in 9:3. In this chapter it moves again to the threshold (v. 4), then rests over the cherubs at the east gate (vv. 18–19). It leaves the city completely in 11:23. This shows that Yahweh was abandoning the temple because of the people’s sin.

### The cherubs and the wheels

The beings and wheels in this chapter are the same ones that Ezekiel saw in chapter 1, where he called them “beings.” Here he says that he realized they were cherubs (v. 20). Translators may want to use the same words for the faces, wings, wheels, and eyes as in chapter 1.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Background information in parentheses

The ULT puts verses 3, 8, and 20–22 in parentheses because they give background information that interrupts the main events. Use whatever way your language has of marking background information.

### Language of approximation

As in chapter 1, Ezekiel uses words such as “likeness,” “appearance,” and “like” to describe what he saw because of the difficulty in describing these unearthly creatures. Preserve this indirect way of speaking so that readers know that he is describing a vision of something that is not of this world.
11:
# Ezekiel 11 General Notes

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Safety

The people were trusting Jerusalem to keep them safe. But God was going to pull them out of Jerusalem. (See: [trust](tw:trust))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Metaphor

The people in Jerusalem used the metaphor “this city is the pot and we are the meat in the pot” meaning they were safe in Jerusalem. (See: [Metaphor](ta:figs-metaphor))
12:
# Ezekiel 12 General Notes

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Exile

God warned that very soon the people in Jerusalem would be exiled to Babylon.
13:
# Ezekiel 13 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

### False prophets

God spoke against people who said they were prophesying but had not received any message from God. (See: [prophet](tw:prophet))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Metaphor

God said of people who encourage others to feel safe even when they continue to sin were not strengthening a wall but just putting whitewash on it to hide the imperfections. (See: [sin](tw:sin); and [Metaphor](ta:figs-metaphor))
14:
# Ezekiel 14 General Notes

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Jerusalem deserves punishment

When the captives from Jerusalem arrive in Babylon, it will be obvious why God has punished them.
15:
# Ezekiel 15 General Notes

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Useless

God said that the people of Jerusalem were useless to him. He uses a simile to show just how useless they were. (See: [Simile](ta:figs-simile))
16:
# Ezekiel 16 General Notes

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Metaphor

God compared Judah to an adulteress because she worshiped idols instead of God who had done so much to help her. Adultery is a common image used to describe the worship of idols by Israel. (See: [Metaphor](ta:figs-metaphor))
17:
# Ezekiel 17 General Notes

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Breaking allegiance

The king of Judah had vowed to obey Babylon but instead he followed Egypt. Therefore, God said he would not prosper. (See: [promise](tw:promise))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Metaphor

Judah is compared to a vine that grows one direction and then another. (See: [Metaphor](ta:figs-metaphor))
18:
# Ezekiel 18 General Notes

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Inherited Guilt

God does not punish children for the sins of their parents, but only punishes them for their own sins. Despite this, the parents’ sins may still have consequences for their children. (See: [sin](tw:sin))
19:
# Ezekiel 19 General Notes

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Judah destroyed

The first king was taken as a captive to Egypt, the next was taken as a captive to Babylon. Now Judah is not prospering.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Metaphor

The kings of Judah are compared to man-eating lions. (See: [Metaphor](ta:figs-metaphor))

# Ezekiel 20 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh refuses to let the elders of Israel inquire of him and instead has Ezekiel recount Israel’s long history of rebellion, followed by a promise of judgment and restoration.

1. The elders come to inquire of Yahweh, and he refuses them (1–4)
2. Yahweh recounts Israel’s rebellion against him (5–29)
    1. In Egypt (5–9)
    2. The first generation in the wilderness (10–17)
    3. The second generation in the wilderness (18–26)
    4. In the land Yahweh gave them (27–29)
3. Yahweh condemns the idolatry of the present generation (30–32)
4. Yahweh promises to judge his people and bring them back to their land (33–44)
5. Yahweh’s message against the forest of the south (45–49)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Acting for the sake of his name

Yahweh repeatedly holds back his punishment so that his name, meaning his reputation, would not be profaned among the nations who had seen him rescue Israel from Egypt. (See: [profane](tw:profane))

### Sabbaths and idols

The chapter presents keeping Yahweh’s Sabbaths as a sign of his relationship with Israel, and worshiping idols at the high places as breaking that relationship. (See: [sabbath](tw:sabbath), [falsegod](tw:falsegod), and [highplaces](tw:highplaces)) Verses 26 and 31 refer to the practice of sacrificing children to idols.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Repeated refrain

Each stage of the history in verses 5–22 follows the same pattern: Yahweh gives a command, the people rebel, Yahweh decides to pour out his anger, and then he holds back for the sake of his name. Translating these repeated expressions consistently will help readers see the pattern.

### Verse numbering

In the Hebrew text, verses 45–49 are numbered as 21:1–5. Translations may follow either numbering system.
21:
# Ezekiel 21 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a series of oracles about the sword that Yahweh sends in judgment, first against Jerusalem and the land of Israel and then against the Ammonites.

1. Yahweh draws his sword against Jerusalem and the land of Israel (1–7)
    1. The sword comes out of its sheath (1–5)
    2. Ezekiel groans as a sign of the coming disaster (6–7)
2. The song of the sword (8–17)
3. The king of Babylon chooses the road to Jerusalem (18–27)
    1. The king uses divination at the fork in the road (18–23)
    2. Yahweh announces judgment on Jerusalem and its prince (24–27)
4. The sword against the Ammonites (28–32)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 21:9–17.

The ULT follows the verse numbering of most English translations. In the Hebrew text, verses 1–32 of this chapter are numbered 21:6–37, because the Hebrew chapter begins with the verses that the ULT numbers as 20:45–49.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The sword of Yahweh

The [sword](tw:sword) in this chapter represents the army of [babylon](tw:babylon) that Yahweh sends to punish his people and the people of [ammon](tw:ammon). Yahweh speaks of it as his own sword to show that he is the one bringing this judgment.

### Divination

In verses 21–22, the king of Babylon uses three kinds of [divination](tw:divination) to decide which city to attack: shaking arrows, consulting household idols, and examining the liver of a sacrificed animal. Yahweh controls even these pagan practices so that the king goes to Jerusalem.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Symbolic actions

Ezekiel groans, strikes his hands together, and marks out two roads as signs to the people (verses 6, 14, and 19). See [Symbolic Action](ta:translate-symaction).

### Difficult Hebrew text

The Hebrew text of verses 10 and 13 is very difficult to understand, and translations differ widely in how they render these verses. The ULT translates the Hebrew literally.
22:
# Ezekiel 22 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter contains three messages from Yahweh that list the sins of Jerusalem and of all Israel and announce his judgment on them.

1. Yahweh accuses Jerusalem, the city of blood (1–16)
    1. Jerusalem’s bloodshed and idols make her guilty and unclean (1–5)
    2. Yahweh lists the sins committed in the city (6–12)
    3. Yahweh will scatter the people among the nations (13–16)
2. Yahweh will melt Israel like metal in a furnace (17–22)
3. All the leaders and people of the land are guilty (23–31)
    1. Prophets, priests, princes, and people have all sinned (23–29)
    2. No one stands in the gap, so Yahweh pours out his wrath (30–31)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The city of blood

Yahweh calls Jerusalem “the city of blood” because many people were murdered there and the leaders used violence to gain wealth. See [bloodshed](tw:bloodshed).

### Refining metal

In verses 18–22, Yahweh compares Israel to the worthless material left over when silver is melted in a [furnace](tw:furnace). Just as a metalworker melts metal with fire, Yahweh will gather his people into Jerusalem and punish them there.

### Holy and common

The priests were supposed to teach the people the difference between what was [holy](tw:holy) and what was common, and between what was clean and unclean. Instead, they profaned Yahweh’s holy things and ignored his Sabbaths, so that Yahweh himself was profaned among them (verse 26). See [profane](tw:profane).

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Shifting references to Jerusalem

In verses 2–16, Yahweh speaks to Jerusalem as a woman, sometimes calling the city “you” and sometimes “her,” and he also speaks of its inhabitants as “they.” In verse 24, he addresses the land in the same way. Consider how to make these shifts clear in your language. See [First, Second or Third Person](ta:figs-123person).
23:
# Ezekiel 23 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is an extended allegory in which Yahweh describes Samaria and Jerusalem as two sisters who became his wives and then were unfaithful to him.

1. Two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, prostitute themselves in Egypt and become Yahweh’s wives (1–4)
2. Oholah (Samaria) lusts after the Assyrians and is punished by them (5–10)
3. Oholibah (Jerusalem) becomes even more corrupt than her sister (11–21)
    1. She lusts after the Assyrians (11–13)
    2. She lusts after the Babylonians and then turns away from them (14–18)
    3. She returns to the prostitution of her youth in Egypt (19–21)
4. Yahweh announces his judgment on Oholibah (22–35)
    1. Her former lovers will attack and humiliate her (22–27)
    2. Yahweh will give her into the hands of those she hates (28–31)
    3. She will drink the cup of her sister (32–34)
    4. She will bear the consequences of forgetting Yahweh (35)
5. Yahweh accuses and judges both sisters (36–49)
    1. They committed adultery, sacrificed their children, and defiled Yahweh’s sanctuary (36–42)
    2. Righteous men will judge them as adulteresses and murderers (43–45)
    3. An assembly will stone them and destroy their houses (46–49)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Prostitution as unfaithfulness to Yahweh

Yahweh pictures his covenant with Israel as a marriage. When Samaria and Jerusalem worshiped idols and trusted in foreign nations such as Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon, it was like a wife committing [adultery](tw:adultery) or acting as a [prostitute](tw:prostitute). See [covenant](tw:covenant) and [falsegod](tw:falsegod).

### The cup of judgment

In verses 31–34, Yahweh speaks of the punishment he will give Jerusalem as a cup that she must drink. The cup is the same punishment that Samaria received, and drinking it will make Jerusalem like a drunken person who suffers horror and desolation.

### Child sacrifice

In verses 37–39, Yahweh accuses the two sisters of killing their children as sacrifices to idols and then coming into his [sanctuary](tw:sanctuary) on the same day, which profaned it. See [profane](tw:profane).

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Oholah and Oholibah

The name “Oholah” means “her tent,” and “Oholibah” means “my tent is in her.” Verse 4 explains that Oholah represents Samaria and Oholibah represents Jerusalem. Consider whether to keep these names throughout the allegory or to explain their meaning in a footnote. See [How to Translate Names](ta:translate-names).

### Sexual language

This chapter uses very explicit sexual language to show how shameful the sins of Samaria and Jerusalem were. If such language would be offensive in your culture, consider using polite expressions that still communicate the seriousness of the sins. See [Euphemism](ta:figs-euphemism).

### Shifts in person

Yahweh speaks about the sisters as “she” and “they” in much of the chapter, but he also addresses Oholibah as “you” beginning in verse 21 and shifts between “you” and “her” in verses 40–44. Consider how to make these shifts clear in your language. See [First, Second or Third Person](ta:figs-123person).
24:
# Ezekiel 24 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter contains Ezekiel’s last messages of judgment against Jerusalem before the city falls, dated to the day the Babylonian army began its siege of the city.

1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to record the date the siege of Jerusalem began (1–2)
2. The parable of the cooking pot (3–14)
    1. The pot is filled with choice meat and boiled (3–5)
    2. Woe to the city of bloodshed, which is like a rusted pot (6–8)
    3. Yahweh will heat the empty pot until its rust burns away (9–12)
    4. Yahweh will not relent in punishing Jerusalem (13–14)
3. The death of Ezekiel’s wife is a sign to the people (15–24)
    1. Yahweh forbids Ezekiel to mourn for his wife (15–18)
    2. Ezekiel explains what his actions mean for the people (19–24)
4. Ezekiel will no longer be mute when a survivor brings news from Jerusalem (25–27)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 24:3–12.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Uncovered blood

The law of Moses required people to cover with dust the blood of animals they killed, and blood left uncovered on a bare rock was thought to call out for vengeance. In 24:7–8, Jerusalem has shed blood openly, so Yahweh leaves that blood exposed as a witness against the city.

### Mourning customs

In this culture, people mourned by removing their turbans and sandals, covering the lower part of their faces, and eating food that neighbors brought to them. Yahweh forbids Ezekiel to do any of these things to show that the people will be too overwhelmed by the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple to mourn properly. (See: [mourn](tw:mourn))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### The cooking pot metaphor

In 24:3–12, the pot represents Jerusalem, the meat represents its people, and the rust represents the city’s persistent guilt. The text moves back and forth between speaking about the pot (“it”) and the city (“her”), so make sure your translation shows that both refer to Jerusalem. (See: [parable](tw:parable))

### Ezekiel as a sign

Ezekiel’s actions in this chapter are a sign that shows the people what will happen to them, and in 24:24 Yahweh refers to Ezekiel by name. In 24:27, Yahweh says that the muteness that began in 3:26 will end when the news of Jerusalem’s fall arrives. (See: [sign](tw:sign))

# Ezekiel 25 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a series of prophecies against the nations around Israel that continues through chapter 32. It contains four short judgment speeches, each against a neighbor that treated Judah’s fall with scorn.

1. Judgment on Ammon (1–7)
    1. Ammon said “Aha!” over the temple, the land, and the exiles (1–5)
    2. Ammon rejoiced with contempt over the land of Israel (6–7)
2. Judgment on Moab (8–11)
3. Judgment on Edom (12–14)
4. Judgment on Philistia (15–17)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Yahweh’s judgment on nations that scorned Judah

Ammon, Moab, Edom, and the Philistines each mocked Judah or took revenge on it when Babylon destroyed the temple and sent the people into exile. Yahweh treats this as an offense against himself and his people, and he declares that he will punish them.

### “You will know that I am Yahweh”

Most of these prophecies end by saying that the punished nation will know that “I am Yahweh.” This shows that the purpose of the judgment is for these nations to recognize Yahweh’s power and authority.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Yahweh tells Ezekiel what to say, Ezekiel’s message quotes Yahweh, and Yahweh quotes what the nations said. Consider whether your language needs to show these levels of quotation in a simpler way.
26:
# Ezekiel 26 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a series of prophecies against the city of Tyre that continues through 28:19. It contains four messages from Yahweh, each beginning with “thus says the Lord Yahweh.”

1. Yahweh will judge Tyre because it rejoiced over the fall of Jerusalem (1–6)
2. Nebuchadnezzar will besiege and destroy Tyre (7–14)
3. The rulers of the coastlands will mourn over Tyre (15–18)
    1. The princes of the sea mourn (15–16)
    2. The princes sing a lament over Tyre (17–18)
4. Yahweh will bring Tyre down to the pit (19–21)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 26:17–18.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Tyre

Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician trading city built on a rocky island just off the coast, with towns that depended on it on the mainland. Other peoples who traded by sea relied on it, so its fall would shock all of the coastlands.

### Mourning for a fallen city

The princes of the sea take off their fine robes, sit on the ground, and sing a funeral song over Tyre. These were common ways to show great grief. (See: [mourn](tw:mourn) and [lament](tw:lament))

### The pit

In verses 19–21, Yahweh speaks of Tyre going down to “the pit” and “the land of the lower parts.” These expressions refer to the place of the dead and indicate that Tyre will be destroyed completely and never exist again. (See: [pit](tw:pit) and [hades](tw:hades))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Changes in how Tyre is referred to

Yahweh speaks to Tyre as “you” but also describes the city as “she” and “her,” sometimes moving from one to the other within a few verses (for example, in verses 3–6 and 17). In the same way, the attackers are called “they” in some verses and “he” (Nebuchadnezzar) in others. Consider whether your language needs to use the same form throughout.

### Quotations within quotations

Yahweh tells Ezekiel what to say, Ezekiel’s message quotes Yahweh, and Yahweh quotes both what Tyre said and what the princes will say. Consider whether your language needs to show these levels of quotation in a simpler way.
27:
# Ezekiel 27 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a funeral song (lament) over the city of Tyre. It continues the prophecies against Tyre that began in chapter 26. Most of the song describes Tyre as a magnificent trading ship that sinks in the middle of the sea.

  1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to sing a lament over Tyre (1–3)
  2. Tyre is pictured as a beautiful ship (4–11)
    1. The ship is built from the finest materials (4–7)
    2. Men from other cities serve as its crew and soldiers (8–11)
  3. The many nations that traded with Tyre (12–25)
  4. The ship is wrecked in the heart of the seas (26–27)
  5. The sailors and the coastlands mourn over Tyre (28–36)
    1. The sailors weep and mourn (28–31)
    2. The sailors sing their own lament over Tyre (32–36)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 27:3–11 and 27:25–36. Verses 12–25 are a list of trading partners written as prose.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Tyre’s sea trade

Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician port whose ships carried goods among many peoples. Verses 12–25 name those peoples and the goods they traded, showing how far Tyre’s trade reached and how rich it had become. (See: [tyre](tw:tyre) and [tarshish](tw:tarshish))

### Mourning customs

In verses 30–31 the sailors throw dust on their heads, roll in ashes, shave their heads, and put on sackcloth. These were common ways to show great grief. (See: [mourn](tw:mourn), [lament](tw:lament), and [sackcloth](tw:sackcloth))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Tyre as a ship

In verses 4–11 and 25–36, Yahweh speaks of the city of Tyre as if it were a ship, describing its planks, mast, sails, rowers, and cargo. The wreck of the ship represents the destruction of the city. If possible, keep this extended metaphor in your translation, since it runs through most of the chapter.

### Place names and trade goods

The chapter lists many places, peoples, and goods that may be unknown in your culture, and the meaning of some of the Hebrew words is uncertain. You may want to use general terms for goods that your readers would not recognize. Additionally the phrasing for trading or buying frequently uses ‘gave,’ you may want to use a more natural term for buying and selling.

### Past tense for future events

Although the sinking of Tyre had not yet happened, verses 26 and 34 describe it as if it were already past. This shows that it will certainly happen. Consider whether your language would express this with a future form.

### They, they
Especially in verses 10-24 pronouns which appear on the verb are also expressed independently. This may have one or more of the follow effects which you may wish to implement in a natural way in your language: 1) marking a new subject (nation) as the topic, 2) creating a list structure, 3) signaling that Tyre’s perfect beauty was actually from all the other nations that traded with her.

# Ezekiel 28 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter concludes the prophecies against Tyre that began in chapter 26. It then gives a short prophecy against Sidon, the neighboring Phoenician city, and ends with a promise that Yahweh will restore Israel to its land.

1. Yahweh condemns the ruler of Tyre for claiming to be a god (1–10)
    1. The ruler’s wisdom and wealth made him proud (1–5)
    2. Foreigners will kill him and bring him down to the pit (6–10)
2. A lament over the king of Tyre (11–19)
    1. The king is pictured as a cherub in Eden, the garden of God (11–15)
    2. Yahweh throws the king down and destroys him (16–19)
3. Yahweh will judge Sidon (20–24)
4. Yahweh will gather Israel and let them live safely in their land (25–26)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter


### Eden and the cherub

In verses 12–16, the lament describes the king of Tyre as if he had been in [eden](tw:eden), covered with precious stones, and as if he had been a guardian [cherubs](tw:cherubs) on the holy mountain of God until he sinned and was thrown out. In addition to being about the king of Tyre, Christians have often viewed this as speaking about the fall of Satan (or Adam), translators should attempt to translate the text as it is and leave the interpretation to others.

### Dying uncircumcised

Dying while uncircumcised implied being an enemy of Yahweh and thus one would go down to “the pit,” which was the place of the dead, perhaps the “bad” part of the place of the dead. This shows that the ruler of Tyre would die like an other enemy of Yahweh. (See: [circumcise](tw:circumcise) and [pit](tw:pit))


## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### The extended picture of the king in verses 12–19

The lament uses a series of images to describe the king’s former glory and his fall: a perfect seal, a garden full of jewels, a cherub, a holy mountain, and stones of fire. If possible, keep these images in your translation rather than explaining each one. The meaning of several Hebrew words in verse 13, including some of the precious stones, is uncertain.

### Quotations within quotations

Yahweh tells Ezekiel what to say, Ezekiel’s message quotes Yahweh, and Yahweh quotes what the ruler of Tyre said. Consider whether your language needs to show these levels of quotation in a simpler way.

# Ezekiel 29 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a series of prophecies against Egypt that continues through chapter 32. It contains two dated messages from Yahweh. The second, given about 16 years after the first, is the latest dated prophecy in the book.

  1. Yahweh will judge Pharaoh and Egypt (1–16)
    1. Pharaoh, the sea monster, will be pulled out of his rivers and left to die (1–5)
    2. Egypt failed Israel like a staff made of reed (6–7)
    3. Egypt will be desolate and its people scattered for 40 years (8–12)
    4. Yahweh will bring the Egyptians back, but only as a lowly kingdom (13–16)
  2. Yahweh gives Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar (17–21)
    1. Nebuchadnezzar received no wages for his campaign against Tyre (17–18)
    2. Egypt will be his army’s wages (19–20)
    3. Yahweh will make a horn sprout for Israel (21)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Pharaoh as a sea monster

Yahweh pictures [pharaoh](tw:pharaoh) as a great creature lying in the Nile, probably like a crocodile, which Yahweh will catch with hooks and throw out to die in the open country. Pharaoh’s claim that he made the Nile, or made himself, was a claim to be a god. (See: [egypt](tw:egypt))

### Trusting in Egypt

The kings of Judah had relied on Egypt for help against Babylon, but Egypt failed them, like a walking stick made of [reed](tw:reed) that breaks and wounds the one who leans on it. After its judgment, Egypt would never again tempt Israel to [trust](tw:trust) in it instead of Yahweh.

### Wages for Nebuchadnezzar

[nebuchadnezzar](tw:nebuchadnezzar) besieged [tyre](tw:tyre) for many years but gained little plunder from it. Yahweh says that he will give Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as payment, because the Babylonian army had been carrying out Yahweh’s judgment.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Yahweh tells Ezekiel what to say, Ezekiel’s message quotes Yahweh, and Yahweh quotes what Pharaoh said, so verse 3 has four levels of quotation. Consider whether your language needs to show these levels in a simpler way. (See: [Quotes within Quotes](ta:figs-quotesinquotes))

### “They will know that I am Yahweh”

This statement occurs four times in the chapter, as it does throughout Ezekiel. Translate it the same way each time.

# Ezekiel 30 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Ezekiel’s prophecies against Egypt. It contains two messages from Yahweh: a long announcement of the day of judgment on Egypt (1–19) and a separate, dated message about Pharaoh’s broken arms (20–26).

1. The day of Yahweh will bring the sword on Egypt and her allies (1–9)
2. Yahweh will use Nebuchadnezzar to destroy Egypt (10–12)
3. Yahweh will judge Egypt’s idols and cities (13–19)
4. Yahweh breaks Pharaoh’s arms and strengthens the king of Babylon (20–26)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The day of Yahweh

In verses 2–3, the “day” that is near is the time when Yahweh comes to judge his enemies, here Egypt and the nations allied with her.

### “They will know that I am Yahweh”

This refrain (verses 8, 19, 25, and 26) states the purpose of the judgment: Egypt will recognize that Yahweh is the true God. Translate it the same way each time.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Nested quotations

The first message (verses 2–19) contains several levels of quotation: Yahweh tells Ezekiel to say what Yahweh says, which includes a command to wail. Consider whether your readers can follow these levels or whether some should be made indirect.

### Names of Egyptian cities

Verses 13–18 name many cities in Egypt to show that the judgment will reach the whole land. Spell these names in a way that fits your language and keep them consistent with how you translated them elsewhere.

### Pharaoh’s broken arms

In verses 21–25, breaking Pharaoh’s arms represents destroying his military power, and strengthening the arms of the king of Babylon represents making his army strong. Keep this image consistent across the section if your readers will understand it.

# Ezekiel 31 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a dated message from Yahweh to Pharaoh. It uses the fall of Assyria, pictured as a great cedar tree, as a warning that Egypt will fall in the same way.

1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to ask Pharaoh whom he is like in his greatness (1–2)
2. Assyria was a magnificent cedar that no other tree could equal (3–9)
3. Yahweh had the cedar cut down because of its pride (10–14)
4. The cedar went down to Sheol, and the nations mourned (15–17)
5. Pharaoh will be brought down like the cedar (18)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### A great tree as a picture of a kingdom

People in the ancient Near East sometimes pictured a powerful kingdom as a huge tree. In this chapter, the birds and animals that live in the cedar and the nations in its shade represent the peoples that Assyria ruled and protected, and the other trees represent other nations and their rulers.

### Sheol and the pit

The “lower land,” “Sheol,” and “the pit” all refer to the place of the dead. The Israelites thought of it as being below the ground, so the dead “go down” to it.

### The uncircumcised

Being buried among “the uncircumcised” (verse 18) was considered a shameful fate, because the Israelites regarded uncircumcised people as unclean and outside of God’s covenant.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Extended metaphor

The whole chapter describes Assyria and Pharaoh as trees. Since Yahweh explains in verse 18 that the picture is about what will happen to Pharaoh and his people, it would be best to keep the tree imagery throughout if your readers will understand it, rather than explaining it verse by verse.

### Who is being addressed

Yahweh speaks to Pharaoh as “you” in verses 2 and 18, but describes Assyria as “it” in between. Make sure your readers can tell that the story about Assyria is told to Pharaoh as a warning about what will happen to him.

# Ezekiel 32 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter contains the last two of Ezekiel’s prophecies against Egypt. Each begins with a date, and both are funeral songs over Pharaoh and his people.

1. A lament over Pharaoh, king of Egypt (1–16)
    1. Yahweh will catch Pharaoh like a sea monster and leave his body for scavengers (1–6)
    2. Yahweh will darken the sky, and the nations will tremble at Egypt’s fall (7–10)
    3. The king of Babylon will destroy Egypt’s people and animals (11–16)
2. Egypt goes down to the realm of the dead (17–32)
    1. Ezekiel is to wail over Egypt and send it down to the pit (17–21)
    2. Assyria, Elam, Meshech, and Tubal already lie there (22–27)
    3. Pharaoh will lie among the uncircumcised (28)
    4. Edom, the princes of the north, and the Sidonians also lie there (29–30)
    5. Pharaoh will see them and be comforted (31–32)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Lamentation

A [lament](tw:lament) was a funeral song sung over the dead. Here Ezekiel sings it over Pharaoh before he dies, which shows that his destruction is certain.

### Sheol and the pit

In 32:17–32, the “pit,” “the lower land,” and [hades](tw:hades) refer to the place of the dead. Ezekiel describes it as a place where defeated nations lie together in their graves.

### The uncircumcised

The Israelites considered it shameful to be buried among people who were not circumcised ([circumcise](tw:circumcise)) or among those killed in battle. Egypt practiced circumcision, so being laid among “the uncircumcised” would have been a great disgrace for Pharaoh.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Yahweh tells Ezekiel what to say, and that message contains further words from Yahweh and from the dead in Sheol. Consider how your language can show these levels of speech clearly.

### Nations and their rulers

In 32:22–30, each nation is referred to as both “her” and “him,” since the text speaks of both the nation and its king. You may need to use one pronoun consistently so readers do not become confused.

# Ezekiel 33 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a new part of the book. Yahweh renews Ezekiel’s role as a watchman, news arrives that Jerusalem has fallen, and Yahweh then gives messages about the people left in the land and about the exiles.

1. Ezekiel is a watchman for Israel (1–9)
    1. The duty of a watchman (1–6)
    2. Yahweh appoints Ezekiel as a watchman (7–9)
2. Yahweh answers the people’s complaints about his justice (10–20)
    1. Yahweh wants the wicked to turn back and live (10–11)
    2. Yahweh judges people by how they are living now (12–16)
    3. Yahweh’s way is fair, but the people’s way is not (17–20)
3. A fugitive reports that Jerusalem has fallen, and Ezekiel can speak again (21–22)
4. Yahweh condemns the people living in the ruins of Israel (23–29)
5. The exiles listen to Ezekiel but do not obey him (30–33)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The watchman

In ancient Israel, a watchman stood on a city wall or tower and blew a shofar (a ram’s horn) to warn the people when an enemy army approached. Yahweh uses this image to show that Ezekiel must warn the people and that each person who hears the warning is responsible to respond to it. Yahweh first gave Ezekiel this role in 3:16–21.

### Turning back from wickedness

Verses 10–20 repeat the teaching of [chapter 18](ta:18). Yahweh judges each person according to whether he is now doing what is [righteous](tw:righteous) or what is [evil](tw:evil), and he wants wicked people to [repent](tw:repent) and live.

### The fall of Jerusalem

The fugitive’s report in verse 21 fulfills what Yahweh told Ezekiel in 24:26–27. Yahweh had kept Ezekiel from speaking freely since 3:26, but now he opens Ezekiel’s mouth.

### The claim to the land

The people left in Judah reasoned that since God gave the land to [abraham](tw:abraham) when he was only one man, he would certainly let them keep it because they were many. Yahweh rejects this claim because they were practicing idolatry, violence, and adultery.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Hypothetical situations

In verses 2–6 and 12–20, Yahweh describes a series of hypothetical situations in order to teach general principles. Use a natural way in your language to introduce these situations. See: [Connect — Hypothetical Conditions](ta:grammar-connect-condition-hypothetical)

### “The righteous” and “the wicked”

Throughout verses 8–19, the ULT uses the adjectives “righteous” and “wicked” as nouns to refer to any person who is righteous or wicked. Your language may need to use a noun phrase such as “a righteous person” or “a wicked person.” See: [Nominal Adjectives](ta:figs-nominaladj)

40:
# Ezekiel 40 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Ezekiel begins his description of his vision of the restored temple which continues through chapter 48. He describes the outer wall, its gates, the outer courtyard, the inner gates, the inner courtyard, rooms in the courtyards, the altar, and the entryway to the temple building.

1. Yahweh brings Ezekiel to see the temple vision (1–4)
2. The man measures the outer wall and eastern gate (5–16)
3. The man measures the outer court and northern gate (17–27)
4. The man measures the inner court and southern gate (28–49)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The temple complex

In this chapter, God takes Ezekiel in a vision to see a restored temple in the land of Israel. As Ezekiel describes this restored temple, he assumes that his readers already know what temple complexes in his culture were generally like. He simply starts describing what he sees, starting from the outer wall and moving in. The temple complex he describes has an outer and an inner wall. There is an outer courtyard between the two walls and an inner courtyard within the inner wall. Each of these walls has three gatehouses in it, one each on the north, east, and south sides. The gatehouses in the outer wall protrude into the outer courtyard. The gatehouses in the inner wall also protrude into the outer courtyard. See below for a description of each gatehouse. There were rooms around the outer wall and a pavement in front of them. There were some rooms near the gatehouses through the inner wall. Within the inner courtyard, there was an altar and the temple building itself. The temple building was on the far west side of the temple complex, which is why there were no gates on this side.

### The gatehouses

Each gatehouse had the same structures and measurements. There were steps leading to the gateway itself. Behind the gateway, there was a hallway that passed through the rest of the structure. On each side of the hallway were three alcoves with low walls in front of them. For the outer gatehouses, the hallway ended in a porch, which opened onto the outer court. For the inner gatehouses, the porch was in front of the hallway so it too could open onto the outer court. Ezekiel learns the measurements and some of the decorations for all these parts of the gatehouse.

### Ezekiel’s guide

In this chapter, Ezekiel’s guide is called “a man” or “he.” Most scholars think that he is an angel. There are many other stories in this culture about angels who guide a human and show special things to that human. However, Ezekiel does not specify anything about this “man” except that he is bright and shining. Consider how you might refer to this “man” without being too specific.

### Long cubits

In verse 5, Ezekiel states that the man’s measuring stick used long cubits. These cubits were the length of a standard cubit plus one handbreadth. Standard cubits were around 46 centimeters long. A handbreadth was about 8 centimeters. So, these long cubits were around 54 centimeters long. This the length of the cubit that Ezekiel uses throughout the rest of this section. The UST expresses the appropriate measurements in centimeters and meters.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Measurement directions

Ezekiel seems to use the word “width” for the shorter side of a shape and the word “length” for the longer side of a shape. This is particularly clear in 40:49 and 41:2. In 40:49, Ezekiel identifies the “length” of the porch as 20 cubits. This measures from the porch from north to south. However, in 41:2, he identifies the “width” of the holy place as 20 cubits. This again measures from north to south. This is not natural in English. Speakers of English usually use the same term for the same compass direction. In this case, an English speaker would probably use “width” for both of these measurements. The ULT follows the Hebrew terms. The UST uses natural English terms. Consider how you might identify directions of measurement in your language.

### Architectural terms and repeated phrases

The exact meaning of some building terms, such as those translated “alcove,” “jamb,” “porch,” and “sill,” is uncertain, and translators may use general terms for parts of a gateway. The chapter also repeats expressions such as “around, around” (all the way around), “from here and from there” (on each side), “whose face was the way of the east” (facing east), and “the way of the east” (east side) which should be translated consistently.

### Corrections of the scribes

In this chapter, later scribes provided many corrections in the margins. Sometimes modern translations follow these corrections, and sometimes they do not. The ULT always follows the traditional consonantal text. The UST sometimes follows the corrections in the margins. In these cases, there are notes that explain the alternative reading.

### Alternative readings

There are several places in this chapter where the traditional Hebrew consonants do not make much sense or do not fit with the other descriptions and measurements in this section. In many of these cases, the ancient Greek translation has a reading that makes more sense. Many translations use the ancient Greek translation in these cases. Translation notes identify these specific cases and provide the alternative readings. The UST often, but not always, follows these alternative readings.

# Ezekiel 41 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

5. Ezekiel brings messages of hope (34–48)
    * Jerusalem and the temple restored (40–48)

In this chapter, Ezekiel learns about the measurements, decorations, and one piece of furniture for the temple building itself. He also learns about the courtyard around the temple building and a structure to the west of the temple building.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Long cubits

In 40:5, Ezekiel states that the man’s measuring stick used long cubits. These cubits were the length of a standard cubit plus one handbreadth. Standard cubits were around 46 centimeters long. A handbreadth was about 8 centimeters. So, these long cubits were around 54 centimeters long. This is the length of the cubit that Ezekiel uses throughout this section. The UST expresses the appropriate measurements in centimeters and meters.

### The temple building

The temple building includes two primary rooms, the “nave” (the Holy Place) and the “holy place” (the Most Holy Place). The Holy Place is a rectangle, and the Most Holy Place behind it to the west is a square. The temple building also has a rectangular entryway. There are side chambers whose back walls butt up against the outside wall of the temple building. The temple building sits on a raised platform or foundation. The whole temple building, including the side chambers, is 100 cubits from east to west and 50 cubits from north to south. (See: [temple](tw:temple))

### The side chambers

There are three stories of side chambers. It is possible that each story was a single, long chamber that went around the outside of the temple building. It is more likely that each story contained 30 individual rooms that went around the outside of the temple building. There is either a ramp or stairs leading to the higher stories. The higher stories are deeper than the lower stories. This may mean that the temple wall narrowed as it went up. It may mean that the upper stories hung over the lower stories. Scholars are not sure what these side rooms were for. They may have been for storing things.

### The courtyard around the temple building

There was a small courtyard around the temple building. On the north, west, and east sides, there were 20 cubits of space between the edge of the temple building platform and the edges of the courtyard. On the east side of the temple building was the main inner courtyard, which is 100 cubits square according to 40:47. (See: [court](tw:court))

### The structure to the west

Ezekiel mentions a “structure” on the west side of the temple building, separated by a small courtyard that is 20 cubits wide. This structure has walls that are five cubits thick. Its exterior measurements are 100 cubits from north to south and 80 cubits from east to west. It is uncertain how tall this building was or what its function was. Most likely, its back wall butted up against the outside wall of the temple complex on the west.

### The altar, or table

In 41:22, Ezekiel refers to an “altar,” but his guide then calls it a “table.” Scholars guess that this is the same kind of table that the priests used in the tabernacle and temple to present the special bread to God. In this sense, it is like an altar, since priests use it to present things to God. (See: [altar](tw:altar))

### The doors

In 41:23–24, Ezekiel describes the doors that close the entrances into the Holy Place and Most Holy Place. For each entrance, there are two sets of doors. Most likely, one set was at the front of the sill or threshold and the other set was at the back, leaving a small space in between. Each set of doors had two panels, which were connected to the side walls by hinges. In this way, the panels could open by swinging toward the walls. Consider how you might refer to this style of door in your language.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Measurement directions

Ezekiel seems to use the word “width” for the shorter side of a shape and the word “length” for the longer side of a shape. See the introduction to chapter 40 for more information. This is not natural in English. Speakers of English usually use the same term for the same compass direction. The ULT follows the Hebrew terms. The UST uses natural English terms. Consider how you might identify directions of measurement in your language.

### Unknown terms

In this chapter, there are many technical terms for parts of buildings. Often, scholars can guess what these terms mean. However, sometimes scholars are not very sure. This is especially true in 41:6–8, 16–17, 21. The ULT and the UST provide one of several possible ways to understand these verses. You may wish to follow a major translation in your area.

### Terminology for temple rooms

Throughout this chapter, Ezekiel refers to the two important rooms in the temple building. He consistently uses “nave” for the Holy Place. He uses several words for the Most Holy Place, including “inside,” “inner,” “inner house,” and “holy place.” The ULT follows the Hebrew. The UST refers directly to the Most Holy Place.

# Ezekiel 42 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Ezekiel learns about rooms that are grouped together into two buildings, one to the northwest of the temple building and one to the southwest of the temple building. He learns that these rooms are for the sacred offerings and clothing. Finally, Ezekiel learns the dimensions of the outer wall of the whole temple complex.

1. The man shows Ezekiel the chambers for the priests (1–14)
2. The man measures the outer boundaries of the temple area (15–20)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The chambers

There are two buildings full of chambers, one to the north and one to the south of the structure and courtyard to the west of the temple building. Scholars agree that these buildings are three stories high, and that the highest story’s rooms are smaller than the rooms in the lower stories. Scholars disagree on many other things about how these buildings were constructed. There is a walkway next to each building, but it is not certain which side of the building it is on. There is a wall near the walkway, but it is not certain exactly where it runs. There are “ledges” on each building, but it is not certain exactly what they look like or what their function is. It is clear that these buildings were for the priests to use while they were interacting with holy places and things. When the meaning of a description is uncertain, consider following a major translation in your area or the reading represented by the UST.

### Holy and common

In this chapter, there is a strong distinction between what is holy, or set apart for God, and what is common, or ordinary. Holy and common places, things, and people are not supposed to mix. Both the wall around the temple complex and the two buildings in this chapter help separate what is holy from what is common.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Alternative readings

There are several places in this chapter where the standard written Hebrew text we have today does not make much sense. Instead, a correction written by a scribe or an ancient translation sometimes makes more sense. In these cases, the notes provide the alternative reading provided by the correction or ancient translation. Consider following a major translation in your area or the reading represented by the UST.

# Ezekiel 43 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Ezekiel sees Yahweh return to the temple. Yahweh then speaks to him. He tells Ezekiel about what the Israelites did wrong in the past what he needs to tell them now about this temple. Then, he tells Ezekiel about the altar and the sacrifices required to consecrate it.

1. The glory of Yahweh returns to the temple (1–12)
2. Yahweh gives instructions for the altar (13–17)
3. Yahweh commands the consecration of the altar (18–27)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Yahweh returns

In this chapter, Ezekiel sees Yahweh’s glory arrive at and enter the temple. This is important in the book of Ezekiel because in chapter 10, Yahweh leaves the temple. When Yahweh leaves it is judgment against the Israelites. So, when Yahweh returns, it is repairing the relationship between the Israelites and Yahweh. Ezekiel says that Yahweh’s glory looked like what he had seen previously. These previous visions are in [Ezekiel 1](ta:01) and [8](ta:08). See those chapters for help in translating terms and ideas in [43:1–5](ta:43).

### The altar

In 43:13–17, the sacrificial altar for the temple is described. Much of this description is difficult for scholars to understand. There are three important decisions that translators need to make. First, is the altar made out of three sections or just two? It is clear that the altar is made up of square sections that are stacked on top of each other. The higher section is two cubits narrower than the section it sits on. What is not clear is whether there are two or three of these sections. The UST models an altar with three sections. Second, how many gutters are there on this altar? It is clear that there is a gutter around the base of the altar. This gutter collects the blood from the animals. This may be the only gutter, or there may be a second gutter at the edge of the highest section of the altar. The UST models an altar with two gutters. Third, 43:17 indicates that one of the sections is 14 cubits on each side. Which section is this? It may be the highest section or the middle section. The UST models an altar which has a 14-cubit square highest section. The altar also has a square area on the top for burning the sacrifices and horns at the four corner of this square area.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Who speaks in 43:13–17?

In 43:13–17, there is information about the shape and measurements of the altar. It is unclear who is gives this information. It could be the “man” who has guided Ezekiel previously. It could be Ezekiel himself, writing down what he learned. It could be Yahweh speaking from the temple. Since it is Yahweh who speaks in both the section before and the section after, the UST indicates that Yahweh speaks 43:13–17.

### Pronouns in 43:19–27

In 43:19–27, Yahweh uses “you” in both singular and plural, “they,” and “he.” The word “you” in the singular refers to Ezekiel, and in the plural it refers to all the Israelites. The pronoun “he” probably refers to any person Ezekiel commissions to do a task. The pronoun “they” probably refers to the priests. The UST models this interpretation. However, some scholars argue that “they,” like “he,” could refer to any person more generally. It is also possible that “you,” while referring to Ezekiel, might mean that Ezekiel needs to have someone else do something instead of doing it himself. Consider following a major translation in your area, or you could follow the interpretation represented by the UST.

### Language of approximation

As in chapter 1, Ezekiel uses words such as “likeness,” “appearance,” and “like” to describe what he saw because of the difficulty in describing these unearthly creatures. Preserve this indirect way of speaking so that readers know that he is describing a vision of something that is not of this world.
